summary: Steve Kaliski frames the talk around a critical architectural separation: discovery and exploration benefit from non-determinism (LLMs leveraging vast information), but credentials, payments, and checkout require determinism. Agents are already economic actors spending tokens with LLM providers, but extending them to transact with arbitrary businesses introduces four risks: wrong place (fake domains), wrong thing (misidentified products or overpriced items), wrong amount (price drift, currency confusion, taxes), and wrong credential (exposed card numbers). The basic approach of letting agents browse sites like humans is slow, finicky, and hard to observe. Stripe's ideal approach binds agents to merchants, enforces spend policies, uses APIs, and provides verifiable identities. Kaliski presents three solutions. First, shared payment tokens: an agent collects a payment credential and shares a scoped, limited token with a seller. The token encodes a mandate limiting use to a specific seller, currency, amount, and time window, enforced by Stripe. The seller still receives brand and last-four digits for risk analysis. The demo shows a $50 charge failing against a $25-mandated token, then a $25 charge succeeding. Second, the machine payments protocol (built with Tempo): tool calls are HTTP requests that can require payment. When an agent hits a protected endpoint, the server returns a 402 status code with an encoded payload describing what to buy, who to pay, and the payment mechanism. The demo shows a curl request failing, receiving payment details (one penny, USD on the Tempo blockchain), agent approval, and a blockchain transaction. Third, the Agent to Commerce Protocol (ACP), built with OpenAI, provides a standard set of APIs and objects for structured checkout flows. It enables product catalogs in JSON with images, descriptions, and pricing, replacing web crawling with programmatic back-and-forth between agent, seller, and PSP. The demo uses Stripe Press (Stripe's bookstore), showing an agent requesting AI book recommendations, receiving structured cart state (line items, base prices, applicable tax, fulfillment options), and completing payment via shared payment tokens. ACP supports diverse payment methods including crypto and cards, and critically the seller remains in control, maintaining customer relationships and receiving risk data. In Q&A, Kaliski addresses recurring budgets via an OAuth-like access/refresh flow for subsequent usage, with multiple scoped tokens possible for higher limits. He confirms Stripe Projects is built on shared payment tokens. On blockchain, Stripe supports multiple networks (Base, Tempo); transaction data lives on-chain with Stripe replicating a product view. The TLDR: non-deterministic discovery with deterministic payments, verifiable parties, and structured negotiation yields a small radius of risk for safe agent-to-business transactions.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Core Thesis
sections.summary: Kaliski introduces himself as a principal engineer at Stripe, formerly leading the issuing team. His central thesis: discovery and exploration benefit from non-determinism, but credentials, payments, and checkout require determinism. This separation of 'how do I find things' from 'how do I transact' is critical.

sections.title: Agents as Economic Actors
sections.summary: Agents already spend money via tokens with LLM providers, proxied through subscriptions. The challenge is enabling spend with other businesses, currencies, and payment methods. Agents are crudely LLM calls plus tool calls, both costing money.

sections.title: Four Problems of Autonomous Spend
sections.summary: The four risks: wrong place (fake domains mimicking real merchants), wrong thing (buying wrong or overpriced items), wrong amount (price drift, currencies, taxes), and wrong credential (exposed card numbers, non-relayable payment methods). Browser-based approaches are slow and unreliable.

sections.title: Ideal Approach and Solutions Overview
sections.summary: Stripe's ideal approach: bind to merchants, enforce spend policies, use APIs for programmatic interaction, and provide verifiable identities. Three solutions are introduced covering credentials, payment flows, and checkout.

sections.title: Shared Payment Tokens
sections.summary: Agents collect payment credentials and share scoped tokens with sellers. Tokens encode mandates limiting use to specific sellers, currencies, amounts, and time windows. Enforcement is by Stripe, works across payment methods, and is auditable. Sellers still receive brand and last-four for risk analysis.

sections.title: Demo: Shared Payment Tokens
sections.summary: Live demo showing an agent Stripe account provisioning a shared payment token from a Visa card with a $25 limit and 30-day expiry scoped to a test seller. A $50 charge fails due to mandate enforcement; a $25 charge succeeds. The token preserves card brand and last-four for the seller's risk systems.

sections.title: Machine Payments Protocol
sections.summary: Built with Tempo, the protocol enables HTTP tool calls to require payment. Protected endpoints return a 402 status code with an encoded payload describing what to buy, who to pay, and the payment mechanism, closing the determinism gap for ephemeral interactions.

sections.title: Demo: Machine Payments Protocol
sections.summary: Live demo: a curl request to a protected server endpoint fails with 402, returning payment details (one penny, USD on Tempo blockchain). The agent approves the payment, the request succeeds, and a transaction lands on the blockchain.

sections.title: Checkout Detail Relay (Introduction)
sections.summary: Kaliski introduces the third problem: agents aren't always buying API calls. Checkout details like tax, purchase restrictions, and quantities must be accurately relayed through the agent proxy to minimize disputes and chargebacks.

sections.title: Agent to Commerce Protocol (ACP)
sections.summary: Built with OpenAI, ACP is a standard set of APIs and objects explaining how checkouts work across the web. It establishes a back-and-forth between agent, seller, and their PSP: every time the agent creates a checkout, updates quantity, or picks shipping, the seller relays back the latest state. ACP covers product catalogs expressed in JSON with images, descriptions, and pricing, replacing web crawling with purely programmatic interaction.

sections.title: Demo: ACP with Stripe Press
sections.summary: Demo using Stripe Press, Stripe's bookstore. The agent requests AI book recommendations and receives a structured product catalog. The agent initiates checkout with buyer info and line items; the seller relays back cart state including base prices, applicable tax, and fulfillment options. As payment methods or shipping change, back-and-forth updates occur. Payment completes via shared payment tokens. The flow is flexible across crypto, cards, and hundreds of payment methods, with the seller maintaining control and receiving risk signals.

sections.title: Conclusion and TLDR
sections.summary: Kaliski summarizes: businesses should make products agent-friendly by exposing APIs rather than only web UIs, maximizing deterministic flows. TLDR: keep discovery non-deterministic, shift payments/checkout/credentials to exclusively deterministic. Non-deterministic planner with constraints, verifiable parties, and structured negotiation yields a small radius of risk for safe agent-to-business payments.

sections.title: Q&A
sections.summary: Q&A covers: blockchain data lives on-chain (Base, Tempo) with Stripe replicating product views; recurring budgets use an OAuth-like access/refresh flow for subsequent usage with multiple scoped tokens possible; Stripe Projects is built on shared payment tokens; no public stats on payment volumes but Stripe is encouraged by adoption.

demonstrations: Shared payment token demo: Agent Stripe account provisions a token from a Visa card with a $25 limit, 30-day expiry, scoped to a specific seller. Seller attempts $50 charge — fails due to mandate enforcement. $25 charge succeeds.

Machine payments protocol demo: Curl request to a protected server endpoint returns 402 with encoded payment payload. Details show cost of one penny, USD on Tempo blockchain. Agent approves payment, request succeeds, transaction lands on blockchain.

ACP demo with Stripe Press: Agent requests AI book recommendations, receives structured product catalog in JSON. Agent initiates checkout with buyer info and line items; seller relays back cart state including base prices, applicable tax, and fulfillment options. Payment completes via shared payment tokens.
limitations: Browsing websites like humans is slow, finicky, and hard to observe outcomes — not suitable for payments.
Pasting card numbers directly is insecure and provides no spend limit enforcement.
Only exposing web UIs increases non-determinism in agent interactions with businesses.
No public stats available on payment volumes for these agent payment systems.
Not all payment methods are universal like credit cards; some are expressed differently.
